subject: English
stem: If I \(\underline{\text{was}}\) you, I would do it at once.
solution: 'If I were you' uses the past subjunctive, which English keeps for a condition that is contrary to fact - the speaker is not, and cannot be, the other person. In such unreal conditions the form is 'were' for every subject, including 'I'. 'Was' is the ordinary past indicative and states a real past fact, so it cannot carry an imaginary condition; 'am' puts the impossible condition in the present as though it were true, and 'would be' belongs in the main clause, not after 'if'. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: They \(\underline{\text{has read}}\) that book for ages.
solution: The subject 'They' is plural, so the singular 'has' is wrong at once. The phrase 'for ages' marks an activity that began in the past and is still going on, and English expresses that with the present perfect continuous, 'have been' plus the -ing form: 'They have been reading that book for ages.' The simple present perfect 'have read' reports a completed act and sits awkwardly with a stretch of time still running; the future continuous loses the link with the past altogether; and the present continuous cannot carry a period reaching back from now. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
optA: The atom sizes in Thomson’s model and Rutherford’s model are of the same order of magnitude.
optB: The electrons are in stable equilibrium in Thomson’s model’s ground state. In Rutherford’s concept, however, electrons always feel a net force.
optC: Thomson’s model predicts the collapse of a classical atom.
optD: The positively charged part of the atom possesses most of the mass in both the models.
solution: In Thomson's model the positive charge is spread uniformly through the whole atom, so an electron displaced from its position feels a restoring force and sits in stable equilibrium. It is Rutherford's nuclear model that runs into trouble: the electron moves in a circular orbit, is therefore continuously accelerating, and by classical electromagnetism must radiate energy, spiral inwards and collapse into the nucleus. So the statement that credits Thomson's model with predicting the collapse of a classical atom is the incorrect one. The other three statements are sound - both models give an atom of the order of \(10^{-10}\) m across, Thomson's electrons are in stable equilibrium while Rutherford's always feel a net force, and in both models nearly all the mass sits with the positive charge. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Verbatim from the NCERT Physics XII Atoms exercise; filed to Chemistry because it heads this paper chemistry run and the subtopic names Thomson/Rutherford/Bohr explicitly. Physics > Modern Physics > Atomic Structure is an equally defensible home.

stem: Which one of the following processes involves chemical reaction?
optA: Storing of oxygen gas under pressure in gas cylinder
optC: Keeping petrol in china dish in open
optD: Heating copper wire in presence of air with high temperature
solution: A chemical reaction produces a new substance with new properties. Storing oxygen under pressure only compresses the gas, liquefying air only changes its state, and petrol left open in a dish merely evaporates - in all three the substance is unchanged and could in principle be recovered as it was, so these are physical changes. Heating a copper wire strongly in air makes the copper combine with atmospheric oxygen, \(2\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CuO}\), and the shiny reddish wire becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide, a new substance. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Reactivity Series and Reactions with Water
stem: Aluminium is used in thermite welding because of which of the following?
optB: Aluminium has more affinity of oxygen.
optC: Aluminium is more strong oxidising agent.
solution: The thermite reaction is \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + 2\mathrm{Al} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\). It works because aluminium holds oxygen much more strongly than iron does, so aluminium strips the oxygen out of iron oxide; the reaction releases a great deal of heat and the iron is set free as a white-hot liquid that runs into the joint and welds it. Aluminium is therefore acting as the reducing agent, not as an oxidising agent, and it is this affinity for oxygen - not its low density and not merely its general reactivity - that the process depends on. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Specific Reactions: Precipitation, Electrolysis and Daily Life
stem: An electrolytic cell consists of which of the following?
solution: In an electrolytic cell the electrodes are connected to an external source of current. The electrode joined to the positive terminal of the source is the anode: it is positively charged, it attracts the anions, and oxidation takes place there. The electrode joined to the negative terminal is the cathode: it is negatively charged, attracts the cations and is where reduction takes place. So the cell has a positively charged anode - the reverse of the sign convention in a galvanic cell. Matches option C.

Consider the following statements.
1. Saturated hydrocarbons will give clean flame while unsaturated hydrocarbons give yellow flame with lots of smoke .
2. Saturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in presence of catalyst like nickel to give unsaturated hydrocarbons. Which one of the following statements is true?
solution: The first statement is correct. Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame because the available oxygen is enough for complete combustion, whereas unsaturated hydrocarbons carry a higher proportion of carbon and burn with a yellow, sooty flame. The second statement has the reaction the wrong way round: it is the unsaturated hydrocarbon that adds hydrogen over a nickel catalyst to give the saturated one, for example \(\mathrm{C_2H_4} + \mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_6}\). A saturated hydrocarbon has only single bonds left and so has nothing to add hydrogen across. Only the first statement is true. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Given below is the atomic number of X. It will form a basic oxide with which of the following?
solution: A basic oxide is formed by a metal. Atomic number 7 is nitrogen and atomic number 17 is chlorine, both non-metals whose oxides are acidic; atomic number 14 is silicon, and its oxide \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) is acidic as well. Atomic number 11 is sodium, which has the configuration 2, 8, 1 - a single electron in the outermost shell, so a reactive metal. It burns in air to give \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}\), and that oxide dissolves in water to give sodium hydroxide, a base. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Mond’s process is used for preparing?
solution: Mond's process refines nickel. Impure nickel is warmed in a stream of carbon monoxide at about 330 K and forms the volatile nickel tetracarbonyl, \(\mathrm{Ni} + 4\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni(CO)}_4\). The vapour is drawn off and then heated to about 450 K, where it decomposes back into pure nickel and carbon monoxide. The impurities do not form volatile carbonyls and are left behind, which is what makes the separation possible. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Tinning of the brass utensils is done in order to
solution: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Both of these metals are attacked by the organic acids present in everyday foods such as curd, tamarind and tomato, and the copper and zinc salts formed in that reaction are poisonous. Coating the inner surface with a thin layer of tin places an unreactive metal between the food and the alloy, so the acids in the food never reach the copper or the zinc. The other reasons offered do not survive examination: tin is a poorer conductor of heat than brass, so the coating cannot be for better heating, and a tinned surface is dull grey rather than ornamental, so it is not for appearance. What the coating protects against is specifically the acid of the food, not ordinary weathering. Matches option B.

This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints A. Tinning puts an unreactive metal between food and alloy. 'Prevent corrosion' is the generic trap: true in a loose sense but not the reason tinning is done to cooking utensils in particular. Tin conducts heat worse than brass and the coating is dull, so the remaining two options are excluded on their own terms.]

stem:
Which of the following is/are the characteristics of matter?
1. Particles of matter have space between them
2. Particles of matter are stationary.
3. Particles of matter attract each other.
Select the correct answer from the code given below:
solution: The particles of matter do have empty space between them, which is why sugar dissolves into water without the volume rising by the full amount added - so the first statement is a characteristic of matter. They also attract one another, and it is this force that holds a solid in a fixed shape and a liquid together in a drop - so the third statement is a characteristic too. The second statement is wrong: the particles are never at rest but move continuously and at random, as diffusion of a scent through a room and Brownian motion both show, and their motion becomes faster as the temperature rises. stem:
When does the ‘rate of evaporation’ increase?
1. An increase in humidity
2. Decrease in surface area
3. An increase with wind speed Select the correct answer from the codes given below.
solution: Evaporation is faster when more molecules can leave the liquid surface and get away from it. If the humidity rises, the air just above the liquid already holds a great deal of water vapour, so molecules return to the liquid almost as fast as they leave and the net rate falls - the first statement is wrong. If the surface area is reduced, fewer molecules are exposed to the air at any moment and the rate falls again - the second statement is wrong. Wind, on the other hand, sweeps the vapour away from just above the surface and keeps the air there dry, so a higher wind speed does raise the rate - the third statement is correct, and it is the only one. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: States of Matter, Phase Changes and Diffusion
stem: What is the correct order of force of attraction?
solution: The three states of matter differ in how strongly their particles pull on one another. In a solid the particles are packed closest together and the force of attraction between them is strongest, which is why a solid keeps both a fixed shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid the particles are a little further apart, so the attraction is weaker: a liquid flows and takes the shape of its vessel but still keeps its volume. In a gas the particles are far apart and the attraction between them is negligible, so a gas spreads out to fill whatever container it is put in. The order is therefore solids first, then liquids, then gases. Matches option B.

stem: Which one of the following is rectified spirit?
solution: Rectified spirit is the product obtained by fractional distillation of fermented liquor. Ethanol and water form a constant-boiling azeotrope at about 95 per cent ethanol, and distillation cannot concentrate the mixture past that point however many times it is repeated - so 95 per cent ethanol is what is sold as rectified spirit. To go beyond it and obtain absolute alcohol the remaining water has to be removed by chemical means, for instance with quicklime. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Common Acids: Names, Formulas and Uses
stem: Which of the following is/are the major components of Aqua Regia?
solution: Aqua regia, meaning 'royal water', is so named because it dissolves the noble metals gold and platinum, which neither of its ingredients can dissolve on its own. It is prepared by mixing concentrated nitric acid with concentrated hydrochloric acid in the ratio one to three by volume. The nitric acid acts as the oxidising agent and converts gold to its ion, while the chloride supplied by the hydrochloric acid immediately ties that ion up as a chloroaurate complex, which removes it from the reaction and keeps the dissolution going. It is this partnership, not either acid alone, that gives the mixture its power. Neither sulphuric acid nor hydrofluoric acid takes any part in it. Matches option A.

1. The kinetic energy of the particles increases.
2. The energy supplied by heat overcomes the forces of attraction between the particles.

subject: Physics
stem: The amount of heat energy that is required to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at atmospheric pressure at its melting point is known as which of the following?
solution: Heat taken in at constant temperature while a solid turns into a liquid is called latent heat, and for one kilogram of the substance at its melting point under atmospheric pressure it is the specific latent heat of fusion. The temperature does not rise while this heat is absorbed because the energy goes into breaking down the ordered arrangement of the solid. Latent heat of vaporisation covers the liquid-to-gas change instead, while melting point and boiling point are temperatures rather than quantities of heat. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: A girl is carrying a school bag of 6 kg mass on her back and moves 200 m on a levelled road. The work done against the gravitational force will be (g = 10 ms–2) ?
solution: Work done by a force is \(W = F s \cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the force and the displacement. The gravitational force on the bag acts vertically downwards, while the girl walks along a levelled road, so her displacement is horizontal and \(\theta = 90^\circ\). Since \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), the work done against gravity is \(W = 6 \times 10 \times 200 \times 0 = 0\). The bag is neither raised nor lowered, so gravity does no work on it. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one of the following is not a unicellular organism ?
solution: Amoeba, Chlamydomonas and Paramecium are each a single cell in which that one cell carries out every life process - movement, feeding, respiration and reproduction. Fungi are not an organism of that kind but a whole kingdom, and its familiar members such as bread mould, Rhizopus and the mushrooms are built of many cells joined into threads called hyphae. Taken as a group, therefore, fungi are not unicellular. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one of the following statement is not correct about parenchyma ?
optA: It is the most common simple permanent tissue.
optB: It consists of relatively specialised cells without thin cell walls.
solution: Parenchyma is indeed the commonest simple permanent tissue, its cells are living, and one of its main functions is to store food, so those three statements are true. The remaining statement is wrong on both of its claims: parenchyma cells are relatively unspecialised, not specialised, and their walls are thin walls of cellulose - the tissue is loosely packed with large intercellular spaces, which is what allows it to store material and to exchange gases. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: How many Joules are contained in 1kWH?
solution: One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a device of power 1 kW running for 1 hour. Converting both to base units, \(1\ \mathrm{kW} = 1000\ \mathrm{W}\) and \(1\ \mathrm{hour} = 3600\ \mathrm{s}\), so energy \(= 1000 \times 3600 = 3600000\ \mathrm{J} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}\). The choice printed as \(36 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}\) is that same number written differently. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Superscripts flattened in every option ("36 x 105 J" for 36 x 10^5 J). The loss is uniform across all four options and recoverable by inspection, but restore the exponents before publishing.

subject: Physics
stem: A particle is moving in a circular path of radius r. What will be the displacement after half a circle?
solution: Displacement is the straight line drawn from the starting point to the finishing point, not the length of the path travelled. After half a circle the particle has moved from one end of a diameter to the other, so its displacement is the diameter, \(2r\). The distance covered along the path is the semicircular arc, \(\pi r\), which is a different and larger quantity. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Greek pi is rendered as the letter p in options (b) and (d) ("pr", "2pr"). Distractors only; the keyed option (c) is clean.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Simple Harmonic Motion and General Waves
stem: It is possible to distinguish between the transverse and longitudinal waves by studying which of the following properties?
solution: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, so the vibration can be confined to one particular plane. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of travel, and there is no choice of plane to confine them to. Confining the vibration to a single plane is what polarisation means, so only a transverse wave can be polarised, and observing polarisation tells the two apart. Interference, diffraction and reflection are shown by waves of both kinds and so cannot distinguish them. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: In which cell Centriole is absent?
solution: A centriole is a short cylinder of microtubules that lies near the nucleus, organises the spindle apparatus during cell division and forms the basal body of cilia and flagella. It is present in animal cells but absent from the cells of higher plants, which assemble their spindle without one and which have neither cilia nor flagella in the body of the plant. Matches option A.

subject: Biology
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bisexual flowers contain both male and female reproductive organs.
2. Unisexual flowers have only one essential floral whorl either androecium or gynoecium.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: A bisexual, or perfect, flower carries both the essential whorls - the androecium of stamens and the gynoecium of carpels - as in hibiscus or mustard, so the first statement is correct. A unisexual flower carries only one of those two essential whorls, either the stamens alone in a staminate flower or the carpels alone in a pistillate flower, as in papaya and in the cucurbits, so the second statement is correct as well. Both statements are true. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
chapter: Fluid Mechanics and Properties of Matter
stem: Equal masses of water and a liquid of density 2 are mixed together, then what is the density of the resultant mixture?
solution: Let the mass of each liquid be \(m\). Water has density \(1\), so its volume is \(m/1 = m\); the other liquid has density \(2\), so its volume is \(m/2\). Mixing conserves both mass and volume, so the mixture has total mass \(2m\) and total volume \(m + m/2 = 3m/2\). Its density is therefore \(\dfrac{2m}{3m/2} = \dfrac{4}{3}\). Note that this is the harmonic mean of the two densities and not their arithmetic mean \(3/2\), because equal masses of the lighter liquid occupy the greater volume and so weigh the average towards the smaller density. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Equal masses, so volumes are in inverse ratio to densities. Taking mass m of each, total mass 2m and total volume m + m/2 = 3m/2, giving density 4/3. This is the harmonic mean of 1 and 2, not the arithmetic mean 3/2, which is the trap option.]

subject: Physics
chapter: Fluid Mechanics and Properties of Matter
stem: The pressure at the bottom of a tank containing a liquid does not depend on which of the following?
solution: The pressure exerted at the bottom of a liquid column is \(P = h\rho g\), where \(h\) is the height of the column, \(\rho\) the density of the liquid and \(g\) the acceleration due to gravity. Height, gravity, and the density that the nature of the liquid fixes all appear in that expression. The area of the base does not appear at all: a wider tank holds more liquid and so presses down with a larger total force, but that force is spread over a proportionately larger area, and the pressure - force per unit area - is unchanged. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: The maximum range of a gun on horizontal terrain is 16 km. What must be the muzzle velocity of the shell?
solution: For a projectile launched with speed \(u\) the range is greatest when the angle of projection is \(45^\circ\), and that maximum range is \(R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^{2}}{g}\). Here \(R_{\max} = 16\ \mathrm{km} = 16000\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^{2}}\), so \(u^{2} = R_{\max}\, g = 16000 \times 10 = 160000\) and \(u = \sqrt{160000} = 400\ \mathrm{m/s}\). Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: A diwali rocket is ejecting 0.05 kg of gases per second at a velocity of 400 m/s. What is the accelerating force on the rocket?
solution: The thrust on a rocket is the rate at which the escaping gases carry momentum away, \(F = v\,\dfrac{dm}{dt}\). Here the exhaust speed is \(v = 400\ \mathrm{m/s}\) and the gases leave at \(\dfrac{dm}{dt} = 0.05\ \mathrm{kg/s}\), so \(F = 400 \times 0.05 = 20\ \mathrm{N}\). The unit matters: since the data are in kilograms and metres per second the answer comes out in newtons, and 20 dynes would be only \(2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N}\), far too small a force to lift a rocket. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: A person is standing in an elevator. In which of the following situations he finds his weight less than actual?
optA: The elevator moves upward with constant acceleration.
optB: The elevator moves downward with constant acceleration.
optC: The elevator moves upward with uniform velocity.
optD: The elevator moves downward with uniform velocity.
solution: The weight a person feels is the normal reaction from the floor of the lift. If the lift has an acceleration \(a\) directed downwards, then for the person \(mg - N = ma\), so \(N = m(g - a)\), which is less than the true weight \(mg\). If the lift accelerates upwards, \(N = m(g + a)\) and the person feels heavier than usual. If the lift moves with uniform velocity, upwards or downwards, the acceleration is zero, \(N = mg\), and the weight felt is exactly the true weight. So the weight felt is less than the actual weight only while the lift is accelerating downwards. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: If temperature of an object is 140°F, then its temperature in centigrade is
solution: The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales are related by \(\dfrac{t_{C}}{5} = \dfrac{t_{F} - 32}{9}\), because \(100\) Celsius degrees span the same interval as \(180\) Fahrenheit degrees and the Fahrenheit ice point is \(32\). Putting \(t_{F} = 140\), \(t_{C} = \dfrac{5}{9}(140 - 32) = \dfrac{5}{9} \times 108 = 60\). The temperature is therefore \(60^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: A man pushes a wall and fails to displace it. He does
solution: In physics work is done only when the point at which the force acts actually moves: \(W = F s \cos\theta\). The man pushes hard on the wall, but the wall does not budge, so the displacement \(s\) is zero and therefore \(W = 0\) no matter how large the force he applies. His muscles do tire, but that energy is spent inside his own body maintaining the contraction and none of it is transferred to the wall. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: Why does a cut diamond sparkle?
optC: Emission of light by the diamond
optD: Absorption of light by the diamond
solution: Diamond has a very high refractive index, about 2.42, and the critical angle that goes with it is only about \(24^\circ\). Light entering the stone strikes the inner faces at angles larger than this, so it is totally internally reflected again and again inside the stone before finally emerging concentrated through the top - which is why a diamond is cut with its faces set at carefully chosen angles. The sparkle is thus light reflected out of the stone, not light emitted or absorbed by it, and hardness has no bearing on how it handles light. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: Myopia is due to which of the following?
solution: In myopia, or short-sightedness, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina instead of on it, so distant objects look blurred while near ones are seen sharply. This happens either because the eyeball has grown too long from front to back or because the curvature of the eye lens is excessive, making its focal length too short. Of the causes offered, elongation of the eyeball is the one that produces myopia; a shortened eyeball gives the opposite defect, hypermetropia, and a general loss of accommodation with age is presbyopia. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: A person is suffering from the defect of astigmatism, due to which of the following?
optA: Distance of the eye lens from retina is increased
optB: Distance of the eye lens from retina is decreased
optD: Power of accommodation of the eye is decreased
solution: In astigmatism the cornea is not perfectly spherical: its curvature is greater in one plane than in the plane at right angles to it. Rays lying in those two planes are therefore brought to a focus at different distances, and the person cannot see the horizontal and the vertical lines of an object sharply at the same moment. It is corrected with a cylindrical lens, which supplies extra power in one plane only. A change in the length of the eyeball produces myopia or hypermetropia instead, and a loss of the power of accommodation produces presbyopia. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational attraction between them
solution: Newton's law of gravitation gives \(F = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\), so the force varies inversely as the square of the separation. Doubling the distance replaces \(r\) by \(2r\), and \((2r)^{2} = 4r^{2}\), so the new force is \(F' = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{4r^{2}} = \dfrac{F}{4}\). The attraction is reduced to a quarter of its earlier value. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: Among which of the following house appliances, is magnet an essential part?
solution: An electric bell works by an electromagnet: current through its coil magnetises the core, which pulls the armature across so that the hammer strikes the gong. A fan and a washing machine each run on an electric motor, and a motor turns only because a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a turning force. Magnetism is therefore essential to the working of all three appliances. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: The terminal voltage of the battery whose emf is 10 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, when connected through external resistance is 4 Ω. 4 10 V 1
solution: The cell drives its current through the external resistance and its own internal resistance in series, so the current is \(I = \dfrac{\text{emf}}{R + r} = \dfrac{10}{4 + 1} = 2\ \mathrm{A}\). The terminal voltage is the potential difference across the external resistance, \(V = IR = 2 \times 4 = 8\ \mathrm{V}\). The same figure follows from \(V = \text{emf} - Ir = 10 - 2 \times 1 = 8\ \mathrm{V}\): the missing \(2\ \mathrm{V}\) is dropped inside the cell. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Stem carries a trailing "10 V" residue, most likely a label lifted off a circuit diagram that was not extracted. The question is fully answerable from the text (I = 10/(4+1) = 2 A, so the terminal voltage is 2 x 4 = 8 V); strip the residue before publishing.

subject: Physics
stem: The resistance of a material is most commonly determined by four factors–length, cross-sectional area, type of material and
solution: The resistance of a conductor is \(R = \rho\,\dfrac{l}{A}\), which accounts for three of the factors named: the length \(l\), the cross-sectional area \(A\) and the resistivity \(\rho\), which depends on the type of material. But resistivity is not a fixed number for a given material - in a metal it rises as the conductor gets hotter, because the more vigorous vibration of the lattice obstructs the flow of electrons. Temperature is therefore the fourth factor. Voltage and current do not alter the resistance; they are linked to it by Ohm's law, and it is their ratio that the resistance is. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: In X-ray emission tubes, X-ray is emitted by the acceleration of which of the following?
solution: In an X-ray tube, electrons boiled off a heated filament are accelerated through a large potential difference towards a metal target. On striking the target they are brought to rest almost instantly, and this very large deceleration - an acceleration in the physical sense - makes them radiate their energy as X-rays. Protons and neutrons are bound in the nuclei of the target and are thousands of times heavier, so they are not set in motion in the tube at all, and it is the free electrons rather than whole atoms that are accelerated across it. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Heat transfer takes place according to which of the following laws?
solution: Heat passes of its own accord from a body at a higher temperature to one at a lower temperature and never in the reverse direction without work being done from outside. It is the second law of thermodynamics that states this one-way character of heat flow, and so it is the law that decides whether heat transfer can take place and in which direction it will go. The first law is a statement of the conservation of energy and would permit heat to pass either way; Newton's law of cooling only gives the rate at which a body loses heat once the flow is already under way; and Newton's second law of motion has nothing to do with heat. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Nuclear DNA replicates in which of the following phases?
solution: The cell cycle runs through G1, then S, then G2, and finally M. Replication of the nuclear DNA takes place during the S, or synthesis, phase of interphase: at the end of it the amount of DNA in the nucleus has doubled and each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. G2 is the gap in which the cell manufactures proteins and prepares for division, and M is the division itself, by which time replication is long complete. Matches option B.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following bacterium causes peptic ulcers ?
solution: Peptic ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori. It is a spiral bacterium that survives the acid of the stomach by burrowing into the mucus lining and by releasing the enzyme urease, which splits urea and neutralises the acid immediately around it. The damage it does to that protective lining is what produces the ulcer. The other three names do not fit: Plasmodium vivax and Trypanosoma are not bacteria at all but protozoan parasites, causing malaria and sleeping sickness respectively, while Staphylococci are bacteria but are responsible for skin infections, boils and food poisoning rather than ulcers. Matches option A.

subject: Biology
stem: People drinking water from a shallow hand pump, are likely to suffer from all of the following diseases except which of the following?
solution: A shallow hand pump draws water from just below the water table, which is the layer most easily reached by sewage seepage and surface waste. Cholera, typhoid and jaundice are all spread by that kind of faecal contamination of water, so a person drinking from a shallow pump is at risk of all three. Fluorosis is different in kind. It is not an infection but a disease of excess fluoride, and fluoride enters water by leaching out of rocks deep below the ground, so it is associated with deep bore wells and tube wells rather than with shallow ones. It is therefore the disease that does not belong in the list. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following rotating of crops will reduce dependence on the use of chemical fertilisers?
solution: Chemical fertilisers are applied mainly to replace the nitrogen that crops draw out of the soil. Leguminous crops such as gram, pea and bean carry Rhizobium bacteria in nodules on their roots, and these bacteria fix nitrogen from the air into a form the soil can hold. Growing a legume in rotation therefore restores soil nitrogen on its own and cuts the need for fertiliser. Of the four pairs offered, only the one containing gram includes a legume. Rice, wheat, potato and chilli are all non-leguminous and only remove nitrogen from the soil, so a rotation built from those crops alone gives no such benefit. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following diseases is caused due to the over-secretion of cortisol hormone?
solution: Cortisol is the principal glucocorticoid secreted by the cortex of the adrenal gland. When it is produced in excess the body shows a characteristic picture: a rounded moon face, a fat pad over the upper back, obesity of the trunk with wasted thin limbs, purple stretch marks on the skin, raised blood sugar and raised blood pressure. This collection of signs is Cushing's syndrome. The opposite fault, too little cortisol and aldosterone, gives Addison's disease with weakness, low blood pressure and darkening of the skin, so it belongs to under-secretion and cannot answer a question about excess. Adrenogenital syndrome arises from excess adrenal androgens rather than from cortisol, and testicular feminisation is a defect of the androgen receptor with no bearing on the adrenal cortex. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (C) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Excess cortisol produces Cushing's syndrome. Addison's disease is the deficiency state and so answers the opposite question; adrenogenital syndrome follows excess adrenal androgens rather than cortisol; testicular feminisation is a receptor defect unrelated to the adrenal cortex.]

subject: Biology
stem: Kidney is the main organ in human body that excretes waste products in the form of urine. Which of the following collects and stores urine in the human body?
solution: Urine is formed continuously by the nephrons of the kidney, so the body needs somewhere to hold it between one act of urination and the next. From each kidney the urine passes down a narrow tube, the ureter, which only conducts it and does not store it. The ureters open into a muscular, highly distensible sac lying in the pelvis, the urinary bladder, and it is here that urine collects and is stored; when roughly three to four hundred millilitres have gathered, the stretching of its wall produces the urge to urinate. Only then is the urine passed out through the urethra, which is a channel of expulsion and holds nothing in reserve. There is no structure called the urinary duct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Urine formed in the kidneys is carried down the ureters and stored in the urinary bladder until voided through the urethra. The urethra only expels and stores nothing; 'urinary duct' is not a recognised structure, the tube from kidney to bladder being the ureter; and since a correct option is present, 'none of these' fails.]

subject: Polity
chapter: Indian Constitution — Making, Foundation and Amendments
subtopic: Making of Constitution and Constitutional History
stem: Which of the following features was not borrowed from the British constitution for the Indian constitution?
optB: The idea of the rule of the law
optC: Institution of the speaker and her/his role
solution: Three of the four features listed are British in origin: the parliamentary form of government with a nominal head of state and a real executive answerable to the legislature, the doctrine of the rule of law, and the office of the Speaker together with the powers attached to it. The Directive Principles of State Policy are the exception. They were taken from the Constitution of Ireland, which had in turn drawn the idea from Spain, and they have no counterpart in Britain, which has no written constitution to place such principles in. Matches option D.

subject: Polity
chapter: Indian Constitution — Making, Foundation and Amendments
subtopic: Making of Constitution and Constitutional History
stem: When was the concept of objective resolution moved in the constituent assembly?
solution: The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on 9 December 1946, and Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution in it four days later, on 13 December 1946. The Resolution set out the aims and philosophy that the Constitution was to embody, and its language later became the basis of the Preamble. The question asks when it was moved, so the answer is 1946. Note the common confusion with 1949, the year the Constitution was adopted, and with 1947, the year in which the Resolution was finally passed, on 22 January. Matches option C.

subject: Polity
chapter: Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Local Governance
stem: Who appoints the Delimitation Commission in India?
solution: Under the Delimitation Acts passed by Parliament, the Delimitation Commission is appointed by the President of India and carries out its work in association with the Election Commission of India. It is a high powered body whose orders cannot be questioned in any court. Its chairperson is a serving or retired judge of the Supreme Court, and its members are the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner nominated by him, together with the State Election Commissioner of the state concerned. The Prime Minister and the Solicitor General have no appointing role at all, and the Chief Justice's only connection is that the chairperson happens to be drawn from the Supreme Court, which is not the same as making the appointment. Matches option B.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem: Consider the following facts about Lok Sabha. (1) The Lok Sabha is elected for a maximum period of five years. (2) As of 2024, there are 514 Lok Sabha constituencies. (3) Representatives for Lok Sabha are elected from each constituency through universal adult suffrage. How many of the given statement(s) is/ are correct?
solution: Take the three statements in turn. Statement (1) is correct: Article 83 fixes the normal term of the Lok Sabha at five years from the date of its first sitting, unless it is dissolved earlier. Statement (2) is wrong: the Lok Sabha has 543 elected constituencies, and that figure was still in force in 2024 because the delimitation of seats has been frozen; 514 was never the number of constituencies. Statement (3) is correct: every constituency returns its member by direct election on the basis of universal adult suffrage, with every citizen aged eighteen and above entitled to vote. Two of the three statements are therefore correct. Matches option B.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
subtopic: Judiciary — Supreme Court and High Courts
stem: Under which article of the Indian Constitution does the President of India appoint the Chief Justice of India?
solution: Article 124 establishes and constitutes the Supreme Court, and clause (2) of that article provides that every judge of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice of India, shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The other articles named deal with quite different matters: Article 121 bars Parliament from discussing the conduct of a judge except on a motion for removal, Article 122 protects proceedings of Parliament from being questioned in court, and Article 126 covers only the appointment of an acting Chief Justice when the office falls vacant or the holder is unable to perform his duties. Matches option B.

subject: Polity
chapter: Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Local Governance
stem: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution?
solution: The right to property was originally a fundamental right, guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31. The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 deleted both of those provisions and re-enacted the guarantee as Article 300A, outside Part III. It survives as a constitutional and legal right, so a person deprived of property without authority of law can still go to court, but it can no longer be enforced by a direct petition to the Supreme Court under Article 32. The other three named in the question, the right to freedom, the right against exploitation and the right to constitutional remedies, all remain among the six fundamental rights in Part III. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Near-match in bank d9356857 -- the same "which is NOT a Fundamental Right" stem, but a different option set and a different answer (the bank keys Right to citizenship; this keys Right to property, which the 44th Amendment removed from Part III).

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
subtopic: Judiciary — Supreme Court and High Courts
stem: Under which of the following articles of the Indian constitution, does the President of India have the power to consult the Supreme Court?
solution: Article 143 confers the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. It allows the President to refer to the Court, for its opinion, any question of law or fact which has arisen or is likely to arise and which is of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the Court's opinion on it. The opinion so given is advisory and not binding on the President. The other articles cover different ground: Article 139 empowers Parliament to confer on the Supreme Court the power to issue certain writs, Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India, and Article 142 lets the Court pass any decree necessary for doing complete justice. Matches option B.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem: Consider the following facts about ‘bill.’ I. A bill is a draft of the proposed law. II. If the Rajya Sabha takes no action on a money bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed III. If it is a money bill, the Rajya Sabha can either approve it or suggest changes but cannot reject it. IV. A money bill can be introduced both in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Which of the following is/ are incorrect?
solution: The question asks which statements are wrong, so each must be tested for falsity rather than for truth. A bill is indeed the draft of a proposed law placed before the legislature, so the first statement is true. Under Article 109, a money bill transmitted to the Rajya Sabha must be returned within fourteen days, and if that house does nothing within the period the bill is deemed to have been passed by both houses, so the second statement is true. The same article confines the Rajya Sabha to making recommendations on a money bill, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject; it may not itself reject or amend the bill, so the third statement is true. A money bill, however, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the recommendation of the President, so the claim that it may be introduced in either house is false. Exactly one statement is incorrect, the fourth. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Polarity: the stem asks which statements are INCORRECT. The first three are true, and only the fourth is false, since a money bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the President's recommendation.]

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem: In India, how many days’ notice must be given before the impeachment of the President is initiated?
solution: The impeachment of the President is governed by Article 61. The charge may be preferred by either House, but the article lays down two safeguards before the resolution can even be moved: the proposal must be signed by at least one fourth of the total members of that House, and at least fourteen days' notice in writing must be given to the President. Only after that notice period can the resolution be moved, and it must then be passed by a majority of not less than two thirds of the total membership of the House. The required notice is therefore fourteen days. Matches option D.

subject: Polity
chapter: Indian Constitution — Making, Foundation and Amendments
subtopic: Federal Structure — States, UTs and Finance
stem: What is the tenure of the Lt. Governor in a Union Territory?
solution: A Union Territory is administered by the President through an Administrator appointed by him under Article 239, and in several Union Territories that Administrator is designated Lieutenant Governor. The office follows the pattern set for a Governor of a state under Article 156, so the normal term is five years, although like a Governor the Lieutenant Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and can be removed or transferred before the term ends. Terms of three, seven or ten years find no support anywhere in the Constitution. Matches option C.

stem: Which of the following States was accorded special status under Article 371-A of the Indian Constitution?
solution: Article 371-A was inserted by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1962, following the Sixteen Point Agreement, and applies to Nagaland. It provides that no Act of Parliament shall apply to the state in respect of Naga religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, the administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, or the ownership and transfer of land and its resources, unless the Legislative Assembly of Nagaland so decides. The other states named are covered elsewhere: Assam by Article 371-B, Mizoram by Article 371-G, and Jammu and Kashmir by the now abrogated Article 370. Matches option B.

subject: History
stem: Which of the following grains was rarely used by Harappans?
solution: The foodgrains recovered in quantity from Harappan sites are wheat, barley, lentils, chickpea and sesame, and these formed the staple crops of the civilisation. Rice is the exception. Finds of rice are rare, confined to a few sites and largely to the Gujarat region and the later phase, so it was not a regular part of the Harappan diet in the way the other grains were. Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: Which of the following is/are incorrect about ‘Great Bath’?
optA: It was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides.
optB: The tank was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum.
optC: It was meant for some kind of a special ritual bath.
optD: There were rooms on five sides, in one of which was a large well.
solution: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro was a large rectangular tank set in a courtyard, with a corridor running along all four sides, so the first description is correct. The tank was made watertight by laying the bricks on edge and sealing them with a mortar of gypsum, so the second description is correct as well. It was almost certainly used for a ritual bath taken by important people on special occasions, so the third is correct. The last statement is the faulty one: there were rooms on three sides of the tank, not five, and one of those rooms contained a large well that supplied the water. The claim also fails on its own terms, since a rectangular courtyard has only four sides and cannot have rooms on five. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Option (d) is the incorrect statement because the Great Bath had rooms on THREE sides, not five -- a one-word change from the NCERT sentence, so the item turns on fine discrimination.

subject: History
stem: Which of the following is correctly matched? (1) Agni- God of Fire (2) Indra- Warrior God (3) Soma- A plant from which a special drink was prepared. Which of the following is correctly matched?
solution: Check each pairing against the Rigvedic evidence. Agni is the god of fire, invoked as the one who carries the offerings placed in the sacrificial fire to the gods, so that pairing holds. Indra is the warrior god, the god of war and of rain, credited with breaking open the waters, and more hymns are addressed to him than to almost any other deity, so that pairing holds too. Soma is indeed a plant, and the juice pressed from it was made into a special drink used in sacrifices, the drink and the plant both being personified as a deity. All three pairings are therefore correct. Matches option D.

subject: History
subtopic: Other Medieval Kingdoms (Chola, Rajput, Ahom, Sikh)
stem: Who among the following was the founder of the Slave Dynasty, the first Muslim dynasty to rule over the Delhi Sultanate in India?
solution: The Slave or Mamluk dynasty was founded in 1206 by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a Turkish slave who had risen to be the general and governor of Muhammad Ghori in India and who took power on Ghori's death. The dynasty is called the Slave dynasty because several of its rulers began life as slaves. Iltutmish was Aibak's own slave and son-in-law and became the third ruler, consolidating what Aibak had begun but not founding it. Razia Sultan was Iltutmish's daughter and came later still, and Akbar belongs to the Mughal dynasty three centuries afterwards. Matches option A.

Filed to Other Medieval Kingdoms as the closest existing fit.

subject: History
stem: Which of the following is Ibn Battuta’s book of travels?
solution: Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan traveller who reached India in the fourteenth century and served for some years as a judge under Muhammad bin Tughlaq. He dictated an account of his journeys across Africa, West Asia, India, China and beyond, and that book, written in Arabic, is the Rihla. The word rihla itself means a journey or a travelogue. The other three titles are not works of his. Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: Who among the following was the first viceroy of India after the transfer of power from the East India Company to the Crown of Queen Victoria?
solution: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the administration of India from the East India Company to the Crown, and the head of the administration, until then styled Governor-General, was additionally given the title of Viceroy as the direct representative of Queen Victoria. Lord Canning, whose full name was Charles John Canning, held the office at that moment and so became the first Viceroy. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal in the Company period, Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General until 1856 and had left India before the transfer, and General Dyer was an army officer of the twentieth century with no such office at all. Matches option B.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: In response to which of the following events was the Swadeshi Movement launched?
solution: Lord Curzon announced the partition of Bengal in 1905, and the Swadeshi and Boycott movement was launched in direct protest against it, calling on people to give up British goods and use Indian made ones instead. The other events named came later and produced different responses: the Rowlatt Act of 1919 led to the Rowlatt Satyagraha, and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of the same year, together with the Khilafat agitation, fed into the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920. Since all three of those postdate 1905, none of them can have caused a movement that had already begun. Matches option A.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Which of the following was a Marathi newspaper started by Bal Gangadhar Tilak?
solution: Bal Gangadhar Tilak launched two newspapers in 1881. Kesari, meaning the lion, was published in Marathi and reached a wide readership in Maharashtra, and it was writing in Kesari that led to his prosecution for sedition. Mahratta was its English language counterpart, aimed at an educated all India audience, so it does not answer a question that asks specifically for the Marathi paper. Swaraj and Bharat were not started by him. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Distractor (c) Mahratta is a real Tilak paper but was the ENGLISH one, so the item needs the language discrimination, not just the name.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Who among the following designed the National Flag of India?
solution: The design that became the national flag of India was the work of Pingali Venkayya, a freedom fighter from Andhra, who presented his design to Mahatma Gandhi in 1921. His flag carried the spinning wheel at the centre, and the version adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947 kept his tricolour and replaced the spinning wheel with the Ashoka Chakra. Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem but did not design the flag. Matches option D.

subject: History
stem: Which of the following is incorrect in the context of the ‘Montague-Chelmsford Reforms’?
optA: These were also known as the Government of India Act, of 1919.
optB: They introduced a bicameral legislature in India.
optC: Indians were given limited franchises based on property, education, and income qualifications.
optD: The governor administered the reserved subjects such as education and health.
solution: The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms were enacted as the Government of India Act of 1919, so the first statement is correct. The Act created a bicameral central legislature made up of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly, so the second is correct. It also extended the franchise to Indians on a limited basis, with property, tax, education and income qualifications deciding who could vote, so the third is correct. The last statement inverts the scheme of dyarchy in the provinces. Subjects were divided into two lists: the reserved subjects, which included law and order, police, land revenue and finance, stayed with the Governor and his executive council, while the transferred subjects, which included education, public health, local self government and agriculture, went to ministers answerable to the legislature. Education and health were therefore transferred subjects, not reserved ones, which makes that statement the incorrect one. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Option (d) is the incorrect statement: under the dyarchy of the 1919 Act, education and health were TRANSFERRED subjects administered by the governor with Indian ministers, while the reserved subjects were finance, police, land revenue and irrigation.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: Who among the following has been appointed as the Director General of SSB?
solution: The Sashastra Seema Bal is a central armed police force guarding the borders with Nepal and Bhutan, and its Director General is a senior officer of the Indian Police Service appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. Amrit Mohan Prasad, an IPS officer, was appointed to head the force. The other three names belong to entirely different fields and could not hold a police command: Tuhin Kanta Pandey is a civil servant of the finance side of government, Kumar Tuhin is a diplomat who headed the Indian Council for Cultural Relations, and Sharath Kamal is a table tennis player. Matches option A.

stem: Which of the following was awarded the best movie at the International Indian Film Academy Awards (IIFA) Awards 2024?
solution: The IIFA Awards of 2024 were held at Yas Island in Abu Dhabi and honoured Hindi films released in 2023. The award for Best Picture went to Animal, and Ranbir Kapoor took Best Actor for the same film. The other titles listed were recognised in different categories rather than as Best Picture: 12th Fail won for direction and for its story, and Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani won in a supporting performance category. stem: Which of the following has been renamed Sri Vijaya Puram?
solution: In September 2024 the Government of India renamed Port Blair, the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, as Sri Vijaya Puram. The new name recalls the Srivijaya empire, whose maritime reach extended to these islands, and the change was made to shed a name inherited from the colonial period. It should not be confused with the earlier renaming of 2018, when Havelock Island became Swaraj Dweep and Neil Island became Shaheed Dweep. Matches option A.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: Where will India’s first Namo Bharat Rapid Rail operate?
solution: The first Namo Bharat Rapid Rail service was flagged off in September 2024 and runs between Ahmedabad and Bhuj in Gujarat. The train had been developed and publicised as the Vande Metro, a short distance intercity service built on the Vande Bharat platform, and was renamed Namo Bharat Rapid Rail at the time of its launch. The Delhi to Meerut corridor is a separate project, the Regional Rapid Transit System, whose trains carry the Namo Bharat name but which is not the Rapid Rail service the question asks about. Matches option C.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: What is the corpus of the AgriSURE Fund launched by the Central government?
solution: AgriSURE, the Agri Fund for Start-Ups and Rural Enterprises, was launched by the Central Government in 2024 as a Category II Alternative Investment Fund to provide equity and debt to agricultural start-ups and rural enterprises. Its corpus is Rs 750 crore, made up of Rs 250 crore contributed by NABARD, Rs 250 crore by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare, and Rs 250 crore raised from other institutions and market participants. Matches option B.

subject: Current Affairs

stem: Which of the following fintech firms has merged and consolidated its operations with North East Small Finance Bank?
solution: Slice, a Bengaluru based fintech firm best known for its card and credit products, merged with the Guwahati based North East Small Finance Bank after receiving approval from the Reserve Bank of India. The merger let the fintech operate under a banking licence instead of applying for one afresh, and the combined entity carries the banking business forward. Jupiter, Cred and Paytm were not part of this transaction. Matches option A.

subject: Current Affairs

stem: Recently, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) partnered with which of the following banks for India’s first blue loan?
solution: A blue loan is financing earmarked for projects that protect water resources and the marine environment, such as water supply, wastewater treatment, water efficiency and the reduction of marine plastic. The International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank Group, extended India's first such loan to Axis Bank, which is on-lending the money to eligible blue projects in the country. Matches option C.

subject: Geography
stem: What is the correct sequence of gases found in the atmosphere on the basis of the percentage in descending order?
solution: By volume, dry air is about 78 per cent nitrogen and about 21 per cent oxygen, and those two together account for roughly 99 per cent of the atmosphere. The largest of the remaining gases is argon at about 0.93 per cent, and carbon dioxide comes next at about 0.04 per cent. Helium and methane are present only in traces, helium at about 0.0005 per cent and methane at about 0.0002 per cent, which puts both of them far below carbon dioxide rather than above it. So any order placing helium or methane in third position is wrong, and so is the order that puts carbon dioxide ahead of argon, since argon is more than twenty times as abundant. The correct descending order is nitrogen, then oxygen, then argon, then carbon dioxide. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Near-match in bank b31cff37 -- the bank asks only which gas is present in the highest percentage, while this asks for the full descending sequence, so it is a harder, distinct item.

subject: Geography
stem:
Consider the following assertions:
1. Nitrogen is the most plentiful gas in the air.
2. When we inhale, we take some amount of nitrogen into our lungs and exhale it.
3. Plants fulfil their need of nitrogen, directly from the air.
Which of the above assertions is/are true?
solution: Test each assertion. The first is true, since nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the air and is by a wide margin its most plentiful gas. The second is also true: nitrogen is drawn into the lungs along with the rest of the air we breathe in and is breathed out again unchanged, because the body has no way of using it. The third is false. Plants do need nitrogen, but they cannot take it directly from the air; it must first be converted into a usable form by bacteria that live in the soil and in the root nodules of leguminous plants, and only then can the roots absorb it. So the first two assertions are true and the third is not. Matches option A.

subject: Geography
stem:
Which of the following combinations is/are right?
1. Winds that blow constantly throughout the year in a particular direction – Local winds
2. Winds that change their direction in different seasons – Seasonal winds
3. Winds that blow only during a particular period of the day or year in a small area – Permanent winds
solution: Winds are grouped into three kinds. Permanent winds, such as the trade winds, the westerlies and the easterlies, blow constantly through the year in one particular direction. Seasonal winds change their direction from one season to another, the monsoon being the standard example. Local winds blow only for a particular part of the day or of the year and only over a small area, as the land and sea breezes and the loo do. Now check the pairings given. The first pairs the description of a permanent wind with the label local wind, so it is wrong. The second correctly pairs a change of direction with the seasons, so it is right. The third pairs the description of a local wind with the label permanent wind, so it is wrong as well; in fact the first and third pairings have simply had their labels exchanged. Only the second is correct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 2: the three definition-to-wind-type pairs are a match list flattened into the stem and should be a GFM pipe table -- note it never prints the words "List I". The stem also has no closing "Select the correct answer" line. Substance: pairing 1 and pairing 3 are swapped (constant year-round winds are PERMANENT winds, and winds confined to a small area and a short period are LOCAL winds), leaving only pairing 2 correct.

subject: Geography
stem:
Read the following assertions carefully:
1. Horizontally the distribution of air pressure is influenced by temperature of air at a given place.
2. The low pressure area is associated with cloudy sky and wet weather.
3. High pressure is associated with clear and sunny skies.
4. Air always moves from high pressure areas to low pressure areas.
Which of the above assertions is/are true?
solution: Take the four assertions one by one. Horizontally, air pressure at a place depends on how warm the air there is, because warm air expands and rises and leaves lower pressure behind while cool air sinks and raises pressure, so the first is true. Where pressure is low, air is rising, and rising air cools, condenses and forms cloud, which brings cloudy skies and wet weather, so the second is true. Where pressure is high, air is sinking, and sinking air warms and its clouds disperse, which gives clear sunny skies, so the third is true. Finally, air flows from where pressure is higher to where it is lower, and that flow is what we call wind, so the fourth is true. All four assertions hold. Matches option D.

subject: Geography
stem:
Which of the following processes is/are included in the water cycle?
1. Evaporation
2. Condensation
3. Precipitation
solution: The water cycle is the closed circulation of water between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land, and each of the three named processes is one of its stages. Heat from the sun turns liquid water at the surface of seas, rivers and soil into vapour, which is evaporation. As that vapour rises it cools, and on cooling it changes back into tiny droplets which gather as cloud, which is condensation. When those droplets coalesce until they are too heavy for the air to support, they fall back to the ground as rain, snow or hail, which is precipitation. Remove any one of the three and the circulation breaks, so none can be excluded. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Evaporation, condensation and precipitation are the three named stages of the water cycle; all three belong to it, so the option naming all of them is correct.]

subject: Geography
stem: The main cause of the origin of tides in the ocean is:
optC: Due to the force of gravity of both the sun and the moon
solution: Tides arise not from gravitational pull as such but from the difference in that pull across the diameter of the earth, and a difference of this kind falls off as the cube of the distance rather than as its square. The sun is enormously more massive than the moon, but it is also about four hundred times further away, and cubing that distance more than cancels its advantage in mass: the moon's tide-raising effect works out at roughly twice the sun's. The sun is not irrelevant, which is why spring tides occur when the sun and the moon pull in line and neap tides when they pull at right angles, but the question asks for the main cause and that is the moon. Currents in sea water are themselves driven by winds and by differences of temperature and salinity, so they are a separate motion of the ocean and not a cause of tides. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED C -> B. Two independent derivations, each made without sight of the printed key, agree against it. This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints C. Basis: The word 'main' is the discriminator. Tide-raising force depends on the difference in pull across the earth and so falls off as the cube of distance; the moon's tide-raising effect is about twice the sun's despite the sun's far greater mass. The option naming both bodies is the answer to 'what causes tides' without the qualifier 'main', and is the likely mis-key; with 'main' present, the moon is the answer.]

subject: Geography
stem: The word tsunami is originated from which language?
solution: Tsunami is a Japanese word, formed from tsu, meaning harbour, and nami, meaning waves, so it literally means harbour waves. The name came from Japanese fishermen, who would return from open sea where they had felt nothing unusual to find their harbour devastated by the wave. The word entered international scientific use from Japanese because Japan, lying along an active plate boundary, experiences such waves frequently. Matches option D.

subject: Geography
stem:
Regarding the human settlements, consider the following assertions:
1. The places where a building or a settlement develops is called a site.
2. The people living in deep forests, hot and cold deserts and mountains often live in permanent settlements.
Which of the above assertions is/are true?
solution: The first assertion is true: the actual place on which a building or a settlement grows up is called its site, and the choice of site is governed by things like water supply, fertile land, level ground and shelter. The second assertion is false, and in fact states the opposite of what happens. People living in deep forests, in hot or cold deserts and in mountainous country generally live in temporary settlements, because they move with their herds or in search of food and their dwellings are made of material that can be put up and taken down easily. Permanent settlements are those in which people build durable houses and stay in one place. Only the first assertion is true. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the numbered statements are flattened into the stem line instead of each starting its own line. Statement 2 is the false one -- people in deep forests, deserts and mountains typically live in TEMPORARY settlements.

subject: Geography
subtopic: World — Rivers, Canals and Water Bodies
stem:
Regarding the waterways, consider the following statements:
1. Waterways are the cheapest for carrying heavy and bulky goods over long distances.
2. Only rivers are used for inland waterways.
Which of the above assertions is/are true?
solution: The first statement is true. Water transport is the cheapest way of moving heavy and bulky cargo over long distances, because the water itself bears the weight of the load and no track or road has to be built or maintained. The second statement is false. Inland waterways are not limited to rivers; canals, lakes and coastal backwaters are all used as inland waterways, and many countries rely heavily on canal systems for inland traffic. Only the first statement is therefore true. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the numbered statements are flattened into the stem line instead of each starting its own line. Filing note: this is general (not India-specific) transport geography; the rivers-and-canals subtopic is the closest fit because statement 2 turns on canals also counting as inland waterways, which is what makes it false.

subject: Geography
chapter: Indian Geography — Economy, Resources and Transport
stem: Which cities of India are connected by the Golden Quadrilateral highway?
solution: The Golden Quadrilateral is a network of four-lane and six-lane national highways, running to roughly 5,800 kilometres, that joins the four largest metropolitan cities of India into a closed loop. Those four cities are Delhi in the north, Mumbai in the west, Chennai in the south and Kolkata in the east, and the project was designed to cut the travel time for freight between them. Patna, Kanpur and Ahmedabad lie on or near the routes but are not the corner cities of the quadrilateral. Matches option D.

subject: Geography
stem:
Consider the following grasslands:
1. Savanna
2. Veld
3. Campos
4. Llanos Which of the above are examples of tropical grasslands?
solution: Tropical grasslands lie on either side of the equator and extend to the limits of the tropical zone, where the grass grows very tall. The Savanna of Africa, the Campos of the Brazilian highlands and the Llanos of the Orinoco basin in Venezuela and Colombia are all grasslands of this kind. The Veld is the odd one out: it lies on the high plateau of South Africa well outside the tropics and is a temperate grassland, in the same family as the Prairies of North America, the Pampas of Argentina, the Steppes of Central Asia and the Downs of Australia. So three of the four named grasslands are tropical and the Veld is not. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the numbered statements are flattened into the stem line instead of each starting its own line. Veld is a TEMPERATE grassland of South Africa, while Savanna, Campos and Llanos are tropical. subject: Geography
stem: Which areas are mentioned in the context of the following features: Limited growth of natural vegetation, only mosses, lichens and very small shrubs are found here. It grows during the very short summer?
solution: The description given, with plant growth limited to mosses, lichens and very small shrubs and confined to a very short summer, is that of tundra vegetation, which is found in the polar region. Growth is restricted there because the ground stays frozen for most of the year and the growing season lasts only a few weeks. The other regions named carry quite different vegetation. Mediterranean areas support citrus fruit, olives and evergreen shrubs. Hot deserts carry cacti, thorny bushes and date palms. A cold desert such as Ladakh or the Gobi is defined by very low rainfall rather than by high latitude and carries scrub, coarse grasses and thorny bushes, not the moss and lichen cover described here. stem:
In the context of temperate grasslands, consider the following assertions:
1. These grasslands are found in the mid- latitudinal zones and in the interior part of the continents.
2. Usually, grass here is short and nutritious.
Which of the above assertions is/are true?
solution: Both assertions are true. Temperate grasslands lie in the middle latitudes, in the interiors of the continents, where distance from the sea keeps rainfall moderate and prevents trees from growing; the Prairies, the Pampas, the Steppes, the Veld and the Downs all occupy such positions. The grass there is short and nutritious, unlike the very tall grass of the tropical savanna, which is why these regions became the great cattle rearing and wheat growing belts of the world. Since both statements hold, both are to be accepted. Matches option C.

subject: Geography
stem:
In the context of tropical grasslands, consider the following assertions:
1. Tropical grasslands occur only in the north of the equator.
2. Tropical grass usually grow very small.
3. Savannah grasslands of Africa are examples of tropical grasslands.
Which of the above assertions is/are false?
solution: The question asks which assertions are false, so each is tested for error. Tropical grasslands lie on either side of the equator and extend towards the tropics: the savanna of Africa straddles it, and the campos of Brazil and the grasslands of northern Australia lie south of it, so the claim that they occur only to the north of the equator is false. Tropical grass is characteristically tall, commonly three to four metres, high enough to conceal a grazing animal, so the claim that it usually grows very small is false as well. The savanna grassland of Africa is the standard textbook example of a tropical grassland, so that assertion is true and is not among the errors. Two assertions are false, the first and the second. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Polarity: the stem asks which assertions are FALSE. Tropical grasslands lie on both sides of the equator, so the first is false; tropical grass grows very tall, commonly three to four metres, so the second is false; the African savanna is the standard example, so the third is true. The false pair is the first and second.]

subject: Geography
stem:
In which part of the continents are Mediterranean vegetation found?
1. Western part
2. Eastern part
3. Southwestern part 4. Northern part
solution: Mediterranean vegetation consists of short evergreen trees and shrubs such as olive, fig and cork oak, with thick bark and small leathery leaves that resist drying. It grows where the summer is hot and dry and the rain falls in winter, and that climate is produced on the western margins of continents between roughly thirty and forty degrees of latitude, where offshore winds and cool coastal currents keep the summer rainless. Besides the lands around the Mediterranean Sea itself, the same vegetation occurs in California on the west coast of North America, in central Chile on the west of South America, and in the south-western corners of Africa and of Australia. The type therefore belongs to the western and the south-western parts of continents; the eastern and northern parts of continents have different climates and carry different vegetation. Matches option A.

Basis: Mediterranean vegetation belongs to the western margins of continents between roughly thirty and forty degrees of latitude, together with the south-western corners of Africa, Australia and South America. So the western and the south-western parts; the eastern and northern parts carry other vegetation types.]

subject: Geography
stem:
In the context of temperate deciduous forests, which of the following assertions is/are true?
1. As we go towards higher latitudes, more temperate deciduous forests are found.
2. They are found mostly in the North-eastern past of USA, and coastal regions of Western Europe.
3. They shed their leaves in the dry season.
solution: Test each assertion in turn. Temperate deciduous forests belong to the middle latitudes, and as one moves polewards out of the tropics and through the warm temperate belt these forests become the dominant type, so the first assertion holds. Their characteristic locations are the north-eastern United States, China, New Zealand, Chile and the coastal belt of western Europe, so the second holds. The defining habit of a deciduous tree such as oak, ash or beech is that it drops all its leaves before the season in which water is hard to draw from the ground, standing bare until growth resumes, which is what the third asserts. Since no assertion fails, all three are true together. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> D. Two independent derivations, each made without sight of the printed key, agree against it. This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints B. Basis: All three assertions are standard school-geography statements about temperate deciduous forests and are printed almost verbatim in the prescribed treatment: that they increase as one moves towards higher latitudes, that they occur in the north-eastern United States and the coastal belt of western Europe, and that they shed their leaves in the dry season. Confidence is medium only because the third is loosely worded scientifically, since such trees shed before winter as much as before drought; if a marker read that as an error the intended key would instead be the option naming the first and second. On the syllabus wording all three stand.]

subject: Geography
stem:
The growth of any vegetation depends on which factors?
1. Temperature
2. Moisture
3. Thickness of soil
4. Wildlife
optD: All of these Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
solution: A plant can grow only where it can obtain warmth and water, so temperature and moisture are the two primary controls, and between them they decide whether a region carries forest, grassland or desert. The soil is the medium the roots occupy, so its depth matters too: a thick soil holds more water and anchors deep roots, supporting tall trees, while a thin soil lying over rock can carry only shrubs and grasses. Wildlife works the other way round, since animals are supported by the plants of a region and depend on them for food and shelter; they do not determine whether those plants can grow there in the first place. The controls on growth are therefore temperature, moisture and the thickness of the soil. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (C) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Growth of vegetation depends primarily on temperature and moisture, and further on the thickness of the soil the roots occupy. Wildlife depends on the vegetation rather than determining it, so the fourth factor is excluded and the answer is the first three.
